title: Minimum Window Substring
summary: You get two strings, `s` and `t`. Find the shortest substring of `s` that contains every character of `t`, counting repeats: if `t` holds two a's, the substring needs at least two a's. Return that substring, or an empty string if no substring of `s` has them all. Letter case matters. When an answer exists, exactly one substring is the shortest.

examples.explanation: "cyab", from index 5 to 8, holds an a, a b and a c. "bxxaxc" at the start holds them too, but it is 6 long.
t needs two a's, so the window must run from the first a to the second: "aya".
s has only one q, and t needs two.

constraints: s and t contain uppercase and lowercase English letters only

approaches.twist: Grow the window until it covers t's counts, then shrink it from the left while it still covers them, keeping the shortest.
For every start, extend the end until the substring covers t's counts, and keep the shortest one found.
approaches.note: Works, but starting over from every index takes O(n²) time, about 10¹⁰ steps for 10⁵ letters. The target is O(n).

signals.meaning: A contiguous stretch that must meet a goal, as short as possible: grow the window until it meets the goal, then shrink it from the left while it still does.
Covering t means having at least as many of each character as t has. Compare counts, and track how many of t's characters are fully covered so the check is O(1).
At most 52 different characters, so the counts take O(1) space however long the strings are.

constraintReading: Both strings can reach 10⁵ characters, so trying every start and extending from it is about 10¹⁰ steps: O(n²) is out. O(n) means each pointer only moves forward, so every character enters the window once and leaves at most once. Counts of at most 52 letters take O(1) space, and keeping a tally of fully covered letters avoids comparing all the counts at every step.

hints.clarify: Does order matter inside the window? No, and other letters may sit in it too; it only needs enough of each character of `t`. Try s = "xaybzab" and t = "ab" by hand: "ayb" (index 1 to 3) holds an a and a b, but "ab" at index 5 is shorter, so the answer is "ab". With t = "aa" you need two a's: "aybza", index 1 to 5.
hints.approach: Sliding window that grows to cover `t`, then shrinks. Count the characters of `t` in `need`. Move `r` right, adding each character to the window's counts, and keep `met`, how many distinct characters of `t` the window holds enough of. When `met` reaches the number of distinct characters in `t`, the window covers `t`: record it if it's the shortest so far, then drop `s[l]` and move `l` right, and repeat while the window still covers `t`. Once it doesn't, go back to growing.
hints.whyNot: Starting from every index and extending until the substring covers `t` is O(n²). Comparing all the counts of the window with `need` at every step works, but it adds up to 52 checks per step; the `met` tally answers "does it cover t?" in O(1). Growing alone can't find the answer: the shortest window usually starts after letters you can drop from the left.

slots.setup: `need`, the counts of `t`; an empty count for the window; `met` = 0, the number of characters of `t` covered so far; `l` = 0; and the best window so far, none yet.
slots.loop: Move `r` across `s` once, adding one character to the window at each step.
slots.update: Add `s[r]` to the window's counts; if its count just reached what `t` needs, `met` goes up by one. While `met` covers all of `t`, remove `s[l]` from the counts, lower `met` if that character now falls short, and move `l` right.
slots.record: Each time the window covers `t`, before shrinking, compare its length `r − l + 1` with the best so far and keep the shorter.
slots.return: Return the best window as a substring, or an empty string if the window never covered `t`.

solution.explanation: `r` moves across `s` once and `l` only ever moves right, so each character enters the window once and leaves at most once: O(n) time, plus O(m) to count `t`. Each step changes one count and maybe `met`, which tells in O(1) whether the window covers `t`. The counts hold at most 52 letters: O(1) space. `met` changes only when a count crosses exactly what `t` needs, so extra copies of a letter never count twice.

events.label: grow
events.say: {c!r} enters the window on the right

events.label: covered
events.say: The window now holds as many {c!r} as t needs: {met + 1} of the {len(need)} different characters of t are covered

events.label: covers
events.say: s[{l}..{r}] covers t, but at {r - l + 1} long it is no shorter than the best so far, {best_len}

events.label: new best
events.say: s[{l}..{r}] covers t and is {r - l + 1} long, the shortest so far

events.label: shrink
events.say: The window covers t, so try a shorter one: drop {out!r} from the left

events.label: lost
events.say: Without that {out!r}, the window is short of what t needs, so stop shrinking and grow again

events.label: not found
events.say: The window never covered t, so there is no answer: return an empty string

events.label: return
events.say: The shortest window that covers t starts at {best_l} and is {best_len} long: {s[best_l : best_l + best_len]!r}

predict.ask: Will this character complete the cover of t?
predict.answerWhen: c in need and window[c] + 1 == need[c] and met + 1 == len(need)

predict.ask: Once this character is dropped, will the window still cover t?
predict.answerWhen: not (out in need and window[out] - 1 < need[out])

related.relation: Also compares a window's letter counts with another string's, but the window has a fixed size and must match the counts exactly.
The mirror image: there you keep the longest window that stays valid; here the shortest window that meets the goal.
